Here's what I'd like to do:

Goal 1: Release Stan 1.0.4 ASAP to fix bugs. The compatibility

and also work without C++11 (including testing w/o C++11).

Require C++11 and use C++11 features.

OR

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: C++11 testing and build statuses
parts:
On Monday, December 10, 2012 12:46:15 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
This brings up some questions:

   Question 1:  If we just turn off all the C++11 features,
   is Stan passing tests on all the platforms it passed tests
   for in version 1.0.3?

At the moment, there are default template parameters (and maybe some other C++11 features, not sure) in some of the tests. If we didn't specify -std=c++0x AND reverted the commits that used C++11 features, I speculate that all the tests would pass. But I think that would be overkill. AFAIK, the only test that is not passing (in some setups) is src/test/gm/parser_test.cpp, which doesn't use any C++11 specific features (that I can see) but doesn't play nice with the intersection of boost and "recent" compilers when -std=c++0x is added to CFLAGS_GTEST (or CFLAGS for that matter).

But that test is somewhat of a luxury because stanc parses everything as long as CFLAGS does not add -std=c++0x. That is why I was proposing restricting the -std=c++0x stuff to CFLAGS_GTEST, blacklisting src/test/gm/parser_test.cpp, doing v1.0.4, and then coming back to it.

Question 2:  How much work do we need to do to back out any
   C++11 dependencies in the new test code?

Not that much, but I don't think it is necessary to back them out. Even if you wanted to do a release with src/test/gm/parser_test.cpp passing, you could just branch from something before 4377102d597c9bd5f011136ea21e6e995c84ac4d. The problem is that you would loose a lot of good commits since then.

Question 3:  Is there some reason (perhaps having to do with
   R, availability on the Mac or Windows, etc) that we can't move
   to always building everything with C++11 flags?

CRAN has discouraging things to say about it

http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-exts.html#Submitting-a-package-to-CRAN

but I am not sure it is prohibited on CRAN. I think g++-4.6 (and the corresponding mingw) just ignores the -std=c++0x thing, but it does implement some features that were later ratified into the C++11 standard. You can see a comparison of compilers here

https://wiki.apache.org/stdcxx/C%2B%2B0xCompilerSupport

My understanding is that the squeekiest wheel is the g++ that comes with Xcode, but I don't really know what to expect from that. We know that the standard C++ library that comes with g++-4.2.x is too old to support any C++11 features (leading to the problem with std::forward that you ran into Friday) but if you use LLVM's C++ library, clang works. So, I don't know what happens if you use the Mac hybrid of LLVM for the first pass and g++-4.2 to finish it with LLVM's C++ library.

But the main thing at the moment is that if you use --std=c++0x to build stanc, then no .stan file parses correctly, but that is independent of R and CRAN.

Question 4:  What versions of clang++ and g++ under what
   backend configs do we need to support?

I'd say the only things we have to support are the compilers on the CRAN servers

http://cran.r-project.org/web/checks/check_flavors.html#r-devel-linux-x86_64-debian

even if RStan never goes onto CRAN. If RStan were to go onto CRAN in some form, then I believe you are only allowed to fail one compiler. Of those, Solaris Studio is already out because it doesn't do boost, eigen, or C++11. GCC 4.6.3 has always been passing on Linux and seems to be passing on Jenkins ATM. GCC 4.7.2 only fails the blacklistable src/test/gm/parser_test.cpp under -std=c++0x.

Clang isn't strictly necessary. But recent versions are the best compilers for Stan, so I think we should be encouraging people to use clang++ rather than contemplating regressions here. Clang isn't systematically slower in runtime, is much better in terms of RAM consumption, compile time, and availability of extra tools, and is a bit better in terms of error messages and completeness of C++11 implementation. Up until today, clang++-3.1 and clang-3.2++ RC had the same test failure as 4.7.2; now they have linker errors rather than test failures with blacklistable src/test/gm/parser_test.cpp.

I just realized it's risky to try to test under C++11 and
run under no C++11.  I'd rather test the same thing we run.

Agreed it would be ideal if it were possible to get everything working with CFLAGS += -std=c++0x, but also working with merely CFLAGS_GTEST += -std=c++0x. For a release and / or CRAN, we could turn off CFLAGS += -std=c++0x and turn on CFLAGS_GTEST += -std=c++0x if necessary.

For the record, as of right now, I can run:

   Platform:
      Mac OS X 10.8.2
   Compiler:
      Apple clang version 4.1 (tags/Apple/clang-421.11.66) (based on LLVM 3.1svn)
   Linker:
      Not even sure what the default is here now that I know

   CFLAGS:
      ?? (I'm running the defaults, but looking at output of "make test-unit", they seem to vary)
      -DBOOST_RESULT_OF_USE_TR1 -DBOOST_NO_DECLTYPE -Wno-unused-function -Wno-tautological-compare
      ?? in building gtest, I also see -std=c++0x and then:
            c1plus: error: unrecognized command line option "-std=c++0x"
   CFLAGS_GTEST:
      ?? (same issue as above -- not sure where the GTEST ones apply)

Look in make/tests, but basically if in make/os_* it says CFLAGS_GTEST += -std=c++0x but not CFLAGS += -std=c++0x, then libstan, stanc, libstanc, etc. implicitly reference -std=g++98 while the tests built by test-unit and test-models explicitly reference -std=c++0x. That would be a decent state of affairs, except that the blacklistable src/test/gm/parser_test.cpp fails for g++-4.7.x and my versions of clang++-3.1 and clang++-3.2.

I haven't figured out a magic set of C++11 flags to let me
compile with g++ on the same platform.

My guess is that many of the tests in test-unit will currently fail with g++-4.2.x if it uses the associated standard C++ library due to complete lack of any C++11 stuff. The thing to try is CFLAGS_GTEST += -stdlib=libc++ (and maybe CFLAGS += -stdlib=libc++), which uses LLVM's standard C++ library (and hopefully is included in Xcode; if not you can download it from llvm.org).

Ben
